newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: SOCCER-AUSTRALIAN FOOTBALL REFLECTS SOCIAL CHANGES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-AUSTRALIAN FOOTBALL REFLECTS SOCIAL CHANGES.

text.p: Former Liverpool midfielder Craig Johnston once succinctly summarised his feelings about playing soccer for Australia.
"Playing football for Australia is like surfing for England," he said during his heyday at Anfield a decade ago.
Johnston preferred to try his luck with England, the country in which he built his reputation, rather than take up a guaranteed place in Australia's national side.

Five failed bids to qualify for the World Cup finals since their sole appearance in 1974 lent weight to Johnston's view of Australian soccer. But now there are growing signs of its emergence as a significant source of playing talent.

Aston Villa goalkeeper Mark Bosnich, charged with misconduct on Monday after giving a Nazi salute to Tottenham Hotspur supporters, Lazio sweeper Paul Okon and West Ham winger Stan Lazaridis head an ever-expanding list of Australian players based overseas.

What began as a trickle a decade ago has become a major exodus. More than 100 players have left for Europe and Asia to work as full-time professionals, an option denied them at home because of the game's shaky finances.
Bosnich, Lazaridis and Okon reflect the social changes which have transformed both Australian society and its soccer.

As descendants of Croatian, Greek and Italian families respectively, they are the products of a post-war influx of immigrants who added Balkan and Mediterranean flair to a traditionally robust English-style game in Australia.

But according to some observers, including Soccer Australia, the sport's governing body, post-war immigration also created a lingering problem which has stunted the game's development as a spectator sport.

Of the 14 semi-professional national league clubs, more than half evolved from within particular ethnic or national communities. Several are now fighting to retain their ethnic character and identity in the face of official policy.
Over the past 18 months, Soccer Australia chairman David Hill has sought to marginalise this ethnic influence.

The Croatian communities in Sydney and Melbourne may follow their own teams, he argues, but other soccer enthusiasts are discouraged by their insularity and fervent nationalism, severely limiting the game's potential.

"We are asking the clubs to take steps to appeal to the broad Australian community," Hill said. "It's all very well for the clubs to say `we're not discriminatory, we do appeal to broader Australia'. They don't."

The latest skirmish in the battle for hearts and minds centred on the inclusion of European national flags in several club logos. Hill wanted them removed. Several clubs -- notably Sydney United, formerly known as Sydney Croatia -- resisted.
Those opposed to the move accused Hill of seeking to deny the clubs their European heritage, with one strident critic accusing him of "ethnic cleansing".

"If we include our national colours in the logo in recognition of those who have given so much to the club, so what? Is that a crime?" asked former Soccer Australia board member Tony Labbozzetta, president of Marconi, a club backed by Sydney's Italian community.
Threatened with expulsion, the clubs backed down. There was no trace of European national symbols on team shirts when the 1996-97 national league season kicked off at the weekend.

Two new clubs -- Perth Glory and Collingwood Warriors, a newly-formed team backed by Collingwood, one of Australia's biggest Australian Rules football clubs -- made their debut, furthering Hill's push for a broader support base.
Attendances have been rising in recent years to reach an average gate of around 4,300 last season. All involved are waiting to see if Hill's reforms boost that.
The opening round of seven matches over the weekend offered Hill some encouragement, attracting more than 40,000 fans including gates of above 10,000 at both Collingwood and Perth.
"The events with Perth and Collingwood are the beginning of the shift upwards of soccer in Australia," a delighted Hill said on Sunday.

Whatever the crowd trends this season, Hill at least has the support of one former critic of Australian soccer: the mop-haired Johnston who eventually failed in his bid to play for England's senior team but won League and F.A. Cup honours at Anfield.
"I'm thrilled to see the game moving towards a more professional footing -- I support the changes 100 percent," Johnston said.
